questions.question: What is the difference between an array and a linked list? When would you prefer one over the other?
questions.idealAnswer: An array stores elements in contiguous memory locations allowing O(1) random access by index, while a linked list stores elements in nodes connected by pointers scattered in memory. Arrays are preferred when you need fast random access and know the size in advance, as they have better cache performance. Linked lists are preferred when you need frequent insertions and deletions at arbitrary positions, as these operations are O(1) once you have a reference to the node, versus O(n) for arrays which require shifting elements.
questions.followUp: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array versus a linked list?

questions.question: Explain the concept of time complexity and Big O notation. Give examples of O(1), O(n), and O(n²) algorithms.
questions.idealAnswer: Time complexity describes how the runtime of an algorithm grows relative to input size. Big O notation represents the upper bound or worst-case growth rate. O(1) is constant time — like accessing an array element by index. O(n) is linear time — like searching for an element in an unsorted array by checking each element. O(n²) is quadratic time — like bubble sort with nested loops comparing each pair of elements. Big O ignores constants and lower-order terms, focusing on the dominant term that determines growth.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between best case, average case, and worst case time complexity?

questions.question: Explain how a hash table works. How are collisions handled?
questions.idealAnswer: A hash table stores key-value pairs using a hash function that maps keys to bucket indices. The hash function computes an index from the key, and the value is stored at that index. Collisions occur when two different keys hash to the same index. Chaining handles collisions by maintaining a linked list at each bucket. Open addressing handles collisions by probing for the next available slot using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing. The load factor (number of entries divided by table size) determines when to resize. Average-case operations are O(1) but can degrade to O(n) in worst case.
questions.followUp: What makes a good hash function?

questions.question: What is a binary search tree (BST)? What are its advantages and when can it become inefficient?
questions.idealAnswer: A BST is a binary tree where each node's left subtree contains only values less than the node, and the right subtree contains only values greater. This property enables efficient searching, insertion, and deletion in O(log n) average time. In-order traversal yields sorted elements. However, a BST becomes inefficient when it degenerates into a skewed tree (essentially a linked list) with all nodes on one side, making operations O(n). This happens when elements are inserted in sorted order. Self-balancing BSTs like AVL trees and Red-Black trees prevent this by maintaining balance.
questions.followUp: How does an AVL tree maintain balance?

questions.question: Explain the quicksort algorithm. What is its time complexity in best, average, and worst cases?
questions.idealAnswer: Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It selects a pivot element, partitions the array so elements smaller than the pivot go to the left and larger ones go to the right, then recursively sorts both partitions. It works in-place without extra memory. The best and average case time complexity is O(n log n). The worst case is O(n²) when the pivot consistently selects the smallest or largest element, such as when the array is already sorted and the first element is chosen as pivot. This can be mitigated by using random pivot selection or median-of-three strategy.
questions.followUp: How does quicksort compare with merge sort in terms of space complexity?

questions.question: What is dynamic programming? Explain with an example problem.
questions.idealAnswer: Dynamic programming is an optimization technique for problems exhibiting overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Instead of recomputing the same subproblems repeatedly, DP stores their results for reuse. There are two approaches: top-down (memoization) which uses recursion with caching, and bottom-up (tabulation) which iteratively builds a table. For example, computing the nth Fibonacci number naively takes O(2^n) time due to redundant calculations, but DP reduces it to O(n) by storing previously computed values. The classic knapsack problem uses DP to find the maximum value of items that fit in a weight limit.
questions.followUp: Can you explain the difference between memoization and tabulation approaches?

questions.question: Explain graph traversal algorithms BFS and DFS. When would you use each?
questions.idealAnswer: BFS (Breadth-First Search) explores all neighbors at the current depth before moving to the next level, using a queue data structure. DFS (Depth-First Search) explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. BFS is ideal for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs and level-order traversal. DFS is useful for detecting cycles, topological sorting, finding connected components, and solving maze problems. BFS guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs while DFS doesn't. Both have O(V+E) time complexity.
questions.followUp: How would you detect a cycle in a directed graph using DFS?

questions.question: What is a heap data structure? Explain its types and applications.
questions.idealAnswer: A heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the heap property. In a max-heap, each parent node is greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum element is at the root. In a min-heap, each parent is less than or equal to its children, so the minimum is at the root. Heaps support O(log n) insertion and extraction of the min/max element. They are commonly implemented as arrays for efficiency. Key applications include priority queues, heap sort, finding k-th largest/smallest elements, merge k sorted lists, and scheduling algorithms.
questions.followUp: How is a heap typically implemented using an array?

questions.question: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm for finding the shortest path in a graph.
questions.idealAnswer: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It uses a greedy approach with a priority queue. Initially, the source distance is 0 and all others are infinity. At each step, it extracts the vertex with the minimum distance, marks it as visited, and relaxes all its edges — updating neighbor distances if a shorter path is found through the current vertex. The algorithm continues until all reachable vertices are processed. With a binary heap, it has O((V + E) log V) time complexity. It does not work with negative edge weights.
questions.followUp: What happens if we use Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with negative edge weights?

questions.question: What is the concept of recursion and how does the call stack work?
questions.idealAnswer: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case (stopping condition) and a recursive case (where it calls itself with modified parameters). The call stack tracks each function call by pushing a new stack frame containing local variables, parameters, and the return address. When the base case is reached, the function starts returning, and frames are popped from the stack. If the base case is never reached, the stack grows indefinitely causing a stack overflow error.
questions.followUp: How can tail recursion optimization help prevent stack overflow?

questions.question: Explain the concept of a trie data structure and its applications.
questions.idealAnswer: A trie (prefix tree) is a tree data structure where each node represents a character of a string. The path from root to a node represents a prefix. Each node has children for each possible next character, and some nodes are marked as end-of-word. Tries enable efficient prefix-based operations: insertion and search take O(m) time where m is the string length, independent of the number of stored strings. Applications include autocomplete systems, spell checkers, IP routing tables, dictionary implementations, and solving word games. Tries trade space for time compared to hash tables.
questions.followUp: How can you optimize the space usage of a trie?

questions.question: What are the different types of balanced binary search trees and why are they important?
questions.idealAnswer: Balanced BSTs maintain a height of O(log n) to ensure efficient operations. AVL trees maintain strict balance where the height difference between left and right subtrees of any node is at most 1, using rotations after insertions and deletions. Red-Black trees use a coloring scheme with looser balance constraints, requiring fewer rotations than AVL trees, making insertions and deletions faster. B-trees are multi-way balanced trees used in databases and file systems, optimized for disk access by storing multiple keys per node. Self-balancing is important because unbalanced BSTs can degrade to O(n) operations.
questions.followUp: In what scenarios would you prefer a Red-Black tree over an AVL tree?

questions.question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST) and what are the time complexities for its basic operations?
questions.idealAnswer: A BST is a binary tree where the left child node is smaller than the parent, and the right child node is greater. In a perfectly balanced BST, search, insertion, and deletion operations take O(log n) time. However, in the worst case (a heavily skewed tree), these operations degrade to O(n) time.
questions.followUp: Name a data structure that prevents a BST from becoming skewed.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS).
questions.idealAnswer: DFS explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, typically using a Stack (or recursion). It is useful for topological sorting and finding connected components. BFS explores all neighbors at the present depth before moving deeper, typically using a Queue. BFS is optimal for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
questions.followUp: Which traversal method requires more memory for a wide, shallow tree?

questions.question: How would you detect a cycle in a linked list?
questions.idealAnswer: The optimal way is using Floyd Cycle-Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare). We use two pointers: a slow pointer that moves one node at a time, and a fast pointer that moves two nodes. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually catch up and lap the slow pointer, meaning they will meet. If the fast pointer reaches null, there is no cycle. This takes O(n) time and O(1) space.

os.name: Operating Systems
os.description: Process management, memory management, file systems, scheduling algorithms, synchronization, and deadlocks.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.idealAnswer: A process is an instance of a running program with its own memory space, file descriptors, and resources. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares the process's memory space and resources with other threads. Threads within the same process can communicate easily through shared memory, while processes require inter-process communication mechanisms like pipes or sockets. Context switching between threads is faster than between processes because threads share the same address space. However, a crash in one thread can affect all threads in the process, while processes are isolated.
questions.followUp: What are the advantages and disadvantages of multithreading?

questions.question: Explain the concept of virtual memory and how paging works.
questions.idealAnswer: Virtual memory creates an illusion of larger memory by using disk space as an extension of RAM. Each process has a virtual address space divided into fixed-size pages, which map to physical memory frames through a page table. When a process accesses a page not in physical memory, a page fault occurs, and the OS loads the required page from disk. A TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) caches recent page table entries for faster translation. Demand paging loads pages only when accessed. Page replacement algorithms like LRU decide which pages to swap out when physical memory is full.
questions.followUp: Explain the LRU page replacement algorithm.

questions.question: What are deadlocks? What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
questions.idealAnswer: A deadlock is a situation where two or more processes are blocked forever, each waiting for a resource held by another process in the set. Four necessary conditions must hold simultaneously: Mutual Exclusion — at least one resource must be held in non-shareable mode. Hold and Wait — a process holding resources can request additional ones. No Preemption — resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process. Circular Wait — there exists a circular chain of processes where each waits for a resource held by the next. Deadlocks can be handled through prevention (eliminating one condition), avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection and recovery, or simply ignoring them.
questions.followUp: Explain the Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance.

questions.question: Explain different CPU scheduling algorithms and their trade-offs.
questions.idealAnswer: FCFS (First Come First Served) is simple but can cause the convoy effect where short processes wait behind long ones. SJF (Shortest Job First) minimizes average waiting time but can cause starvation of longer processes and requires knowing burst times. Round Robin assigns a time quantum and cycles through processes, providing fair sharing and good response time for interactive systems but with higher context switching overhead. Priority scheduling serves highest priority processes first but can cause starvation, mitigated by aging. Multilevel feedback queues combine these approaches for practical systems.
questions.followUp: How does the time quantum value affect Round Robin scheduling?

questions.question: What is a semaphore? How is it used for process synchronization?
questions.idealAnswer: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive that controls access to shared resources using an integer variable and two atomic operations: wait (P/down) which decrements the value and blocks if it becomes negative, and signal (V/up) which increments the value and wakes a blocked process. Binary semaphores (0 or 1) act like mutexes for mutual exclusion of critical sections. Counting semaphores can have values greater than 1 and control access to a pool of resources. They solve classic synchronization problems like the producer-consumer problem. Operations must be atomic to prevent race conditions.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between a semaphore and a mutex?

questions.question: Explain the difference between user mode and kernel mode in an operating system.
questions.idealAnswer: User mode and kernel mode are two privilege levels that protect the OS. In user mode, processes run with restricted access — they cannot directly access hardware, memory management, or other critical resources. In kernel mode, the OS has full access to all hardware and memory. When a user process needs OS services, it makes a system call which triggers a trap (mode switch) from user to kernel mode. After the OS completes the request, it switches back to user mode. This separation prevents user programs from crashing the system or accessing other processes' memory, enforcing security and stability.
questions.followUp: What happens during a system call at the hardware level?

questions.question: What is thrashing and how can it be prevented?
questions.idealAnswer: Thrashing occurs when a system spends more time swapping pages between memory and disk than executing actual processes. It happens when the degree of multiprogramming is too high and processes don't have enough frames to hold their working set. CPU utilization drops dramatically as processes continuously page fault. Prevention strategies include the working set model (tracking the set of pages a process is actively using and ensuring they stay in memory), controlling the degree of multiprogramming, using page fault frequency to adjust frame allocation, and local replacement policies that prevent one process from stealing frames from others.
questions.followUp: How does the working set model determine the appropriate number of frames for a process?

questions.question: Explain the concept of file systems and how files are stored on disk.
questions.idealAnswer: A file system organizes and stores files on disk. Files are broken into fixed-size blocks stored across the disk. The file system maintains metadata about each file (size, permissions, timestamps, block locations) in structures like inodes (Unix) or MFT entries (NTFS). Block allocation methods include contiguous allocation (fast but causes fragmentation), linked allocation (blocks contain pointers to next block), and indexed allocation (an index block stores all block addresses). Directories map filenames to file metadata. Free space is tracked using bitmaps or linked lists. Modern file systems like ext4 and NTFS use journaling to prevent data corruption during crashes.
questions.followUp: What is journaling in file systems and why is it important?

questions.question: What is a context switch and what overhead does it involve?
questions.idealAnswer: A context switch is the mechanism of saving the state of the current running process and loading the state of another process to run. The OS saves the current process's CPU registers, program counter, stack pointer, and other state information into its Process Control Block (PCB), then loads the saved state of the new process from its PCB. The overhead includes the time to save and restore registers, flush and reload TLB entries, cache pollution (the new process's data won't be in cache initially), and pipeline flush in modern CPUs. Context switches are pure overhead — no useful work is done during them.
questions.followUp: How do modern operating systems minimize context switch overhead?

questions.question: Explain inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms.
questions.idealAnswer: IPC allows processes to exchange data and synchronize. Pipes provide unidirectional byte stream communication between related processes. Named pipes (FIFOs) allow communication between unrelated processes. Message queues allow structured message passing with priorities. Shared memory is the fastest IPC method where processes map the same physical memory into their address spaces, but requires synchronization. Sockets enable communication between processes on different machines over a network. Signals are asynchronous notifications sent to processes. The choice depends on requirements: shared memory for high throughput, message queues for structured data, sockets for networked communication.

questions.question: What is the Convoy Effect in FCFS scheduling and how does it impact performance?
questions.idealAnswer: The Convoy Effect occurs in First Come First Served (FCFS) scheduling when a CPU-bound process with a long burst time gets the CPU, causing many shorter I/O-bound processes to wait behind it. This drastically increases the average waiting time and decreases CPU and I/O device utilization.

questions.question: Explain Multilevel Queue Scheduling.
questions.idealAnswer: Multilevel Queue Scheduling partitions the ready queue into multiple separate queues based on process priority or type (e.g., system, interactive, batch). Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm (like Round Robin for interactive and FCFS for batch), and there is scheduling between the queues, typically strict priority preemptive scheduling.

questions.question: What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
questions.idealAnswer: The four Coffman conditions are: 1) Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be non-shareable. 2) Hold and Wait: A process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes. 3) No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process. 4) Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes exists, where each process holds at least one resource needed by the next process in the chain.

questions.question: What is the difference between Internal and External Fragmentation?
questions.idealAnswer: Internal fragmentation happens when a process is allocated more memory than it needs, usually because memory is divided into fixed-sized blocks (like pages), leaving wasted space inside the allocated block. External fragmentation occurs when there is enough total free memory to satisfy a request, but it is not contiguous, meaning it cannot be allocated (common in segmentation or variable partitioning).

questions.question: What is database normalization? Explain the first three normal forms.
questions.idealAnswer: Normalization is the process of organizing database tables to reduce redundancy and avoid insertion, update, and deletion anomalies. First Normal Form (1NF) requires that all attributes contain only atomic (indivisible) values and each record is unique. Second Normal Form (2NF) requires 1NF plus no partial dependencies — all non-key attributes must depend on the entire primary key, not just part of it. Third Normal Form (3NF) requires 2NF plus no transitive dependencies — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes. Each higher normal form builds on the previous one to further eliminate redundancy.
questions.followUp: What is BCNF and how does it differ from 3NF?

questions.question: Explain ACID properties in database transactions.
questions.idealAnswer: ACID properties ensure reliable transaction processing. Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing — either all operations complete or none do, using rollback if any part fails. Consistency ensures the database moves from one valid state to another, maintaining all integrity constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other, as if they run serially — achieved through mechanisms like locks and MVCC. Durability guarantees that once a transaction is committed, its changes persist even after system failures, typically through write-ahead logging. These properties are fundamental to maintaining data integrity in databases.
questions.followUp: What are the different levels of transaction isolation?

questions.question: What are indexes in databases and how do they improve query performance?
questions.idealAnswer: Database indexes are data structures that speed up data retrieval by maintaining sorted references to table rows. The most common type is a B-tree index, which maintains a balanced tree structure allowing O(log n) lookups. Hash indexes provide O(1) lookups for exact match queries. A clustered index determines the physical order of data in the table (one per table), while non-clustered indexes maintain a separate structure pointing to data rows. Indexes dramatically improve SELECT query performance but add overhead to INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations as the index must be updated. Over-indexing can degrade write performance and waste storage.
questions.followUp: When should you avoid creating an index?

questions.question: Explain the different types of SQL joins with examples.
questions.idealAnswer: SQL joins combine rows from two or more tables based on related columns. INNER JOIN returns only rows where there is a match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right table (NULL where no match). RIGHT JOIN is the opposite — all rows from the right table with matching left rows. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with NULLs where there is no match. CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product of both tables (every combination of rows). Self-join joins a table with itself, useful for hierarchical data.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between JOIN conditions in ON clause versus WHERE clause?

questions.question: What are stored procedures and triggers? When should you use them?
questions.idealAnswer: Stored procedures are precompiled SQL programs stored in the database that accept parameters, perform operations, and return results. They improve performance through precompilation, reduce network traffic by executing logic on the server, enhance security by encapsulating operations, and promote code reuse. Triggers are special procedures that automatically execute in response to specific database events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table. They can fire BEFORE or AFTER the event. Triggers are useful for maintaining audit logs, enforcing complex business rules, and keeping derived data synchronized. However, overusing triggers can make debugging difficult and impact performance.
questions.followUp: What are the disadvantages of using too many triggers?

questions.question: Explain the concept of database sharding and when it is used.
questions.idealAnswer: Database sharding is a horizontal partitioning technique that distributes data across multiple database instances (shards) to improve scalability and performance. Each shard holds a subset of the data, determined by a shard key (such as user ID ranges or geographic region). Sharding enables horizontal scaling — adding more servers to handle increased load. It is used when a single database server cannot handle the read/write volume, storage requirements, or query load. However, sharding adds complexity: cross-shard queries are expensive, maintaining consistency across shards is challenging, and rebalancing shards when data grows unevenly requires careful planning.
questions.followUp: What are the different sharding strategies and their trade-offs?

questions.question: Compare SQL and NoSQL databases. When would you choose one over the other?
questions.idealAnswer: SQL databases are relational, use structured schemas, support ACID transactions, and are ideal for complex queries with joins. They scale vertically and excel at maintaining data integrity. NoSQL databases are non-relational, offer flexible schemas, and prioritize horizontal scalability and performance. Types include document stores (MongoDB), key-value stores (Redis), column-family (Cassandra), and graph databases (Neo4j). Choose SQL for structured data with complex relationships, financial applications requiring strict consistency, and when schema is well-defined. Choose NoSQL for rapidly evolving schemas, large-scale distributed systems, high write throughput, and when eventual consistency is acceptable.
questions.followUp: What is the CAP theorem and how does it relate to NoSQL databases?

questions.question: What is query optimization and how does a database query optimizer work?
questions.idealAnswer: Query optimization is the process of determining the most efficient execution plan for a SQL query. The query optimizer analyzes multiple possible execution plans and selects the one with the lowest estimated cost. It considers factors like available indexes, table statistics, join algorithms, and data distribution. Cost-based optimizers estimate I/O and CPU costs using table cardinality and selectivity statistics. Key optimization techniques include index selection, join order optimization, predicate pushdown, query rewriting, and parallelization. The EXPLAIN command shows the chosen execution plan. Keeping statistics up-to-date and writing efficient queries help the optimizer make better decisions.

questions.idealAnswer: ACID stands for Atomicity (all operations in a transaction succeed or fail together as a unit), Consistency (the database remains in a valid state before and after the transaction), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other), and Durability (once a transaction commits, the changes are permanent even in case of a system crash).

A non-clustered index maintains a separate logical structure with pointers to the actual data rows, meaning you can have multiple non-clustered indexes per table.

questions.question: Explain the OSI model and its seven layers.
questions.idealAnswer: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a conceptual framework with seven layers that standardize network communication. Layer 1 (Physical) handles raw bit transmission over physical media. Layer 2 (Data Link) provides node-to-node data transfer with framing and MAC addresses. Layer 3 (Network) handles routing and logical addressing using IP addresses. Layer 4 (Transport) provides end-to-end communication with TCP (reliable) or UDP (fast). Layer 5 (Session) manages sessions between applications. Layer 6 (Presentation) handles data formatting, encryption, and compression. Layer 7 (Application) provides network services to user applications. Data is encapsulated with headers as it moves down the layers.
questions.followUp: How does the TCP/IP model differ from the OSI model?

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP? When would you use each?
questions.idealAnswer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is connection-oriented, providing reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery through three-way handshake, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control. It guarantees all data arrives correctly but has higher overhead. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless, providing fast, best-effort delivery with minimal overhead — no handshake, no acknowledgments, no guaranteed ordering. TCP is used for web browsing (HTTP), email, file transfers — anything requiring complete and ordered delivery. UDP is used for real-time applications like video streaming, online gaming, VoIP, and DNS queries where speed matters more than reliability.
questions.followUp: Explain the TCP three-way handshake process.

questions.question: How does DNS work? Explain the DNS resolution process.
questions.idealAnswer: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names to IP addresses. When a user enters a URL, the DNS resolver (usually provided by the ISP) checks its cache first. If not cached, it performs a recursive or iterative lookup: querying a root DNS server which directs to the appropriate TLD (Top-Level Domain) server (like .com), which directs to the authoritative name server for the specific domain, which returns the IP address. The result is cached at each level with a TTL (time to live). DNS uses a hierarchical structure, distributing the load across thousands of servers worldwide for scalability and reliability.
questions.followUp: What are the different types of DNS records?

questions.question: Explain how HTTPS works and what role SSL/TLS plays in securing web communication.
questions.idealAnswer: HTTPS uses SSL/TLS to encrypt HTTP communication. The process begins with a TLS handshake: the client sends supported cipher suites, the server responds with its digital certificate containing its public key. The client verifies the certificate against trusted Certificate Authorities. They perform a key exchange (using asymmetric cryptography like RSA or Diffie-Hellman) to agree on a shared session key. Subsequent data is encrypted using fast symmetric encryption with this session key. TLS provides confidentiality (encryption prevents eavesdropping), integrity (message authentication codes detect tampering), and authentication (certificates verify server identity).
questions.followUp: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?

questions.question: What is subnetting and why is it used?
questions.idealAnswer: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller, manageable sub-networks. A subnet mask determines which portion of an IP address identifies the network and which identifies the host. CIDR notation (like /24) indicates the number of network bits. Subnetting is used to reduce broadcast domain size (improving performance), organize networks logically (separating departments), improve security (isolating sensitive systems), and make efficient use of IP address space. For example, a /24 subnet (255.255.255.0) provides 254 usable host addresses. Routing between subnets requires a router, enabling traffic control and filtering.
questions.followUp: Given a /26 subnet, how many usable host addresses are available?

questions.question: Explain the concept of routing and different routing algorithms.
questions.idealAnswer: Routing is the process of selecting paths in a network to forward packets from source to destination. Routers maintain routing tables that map destination networks to next-hop addresses and interfaces. Static routing uses manually configured routes, while dynamic routing uses algorithms to automatically discover and update routes. Distance vector algorithms (like RIP) share routing tables with neighbors and use hop count as the metric, but converge slowly and suffer from count-to-infinity. Link state algorithms (like OSPF) build a complete network topology map using Dijkstra's algorithm, offering faster convergence. BGP is the protocol used for routing between autonomous systems on the internet.
questions.followUp: What is the count-to-infinity problem in distance vector routing?

questions.question: What is a firewall and what are its types?
questions.idealAnswer: A firewall is a network security device that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules. Packet filtering firewalls examine individual packets against rules based on IP addresses, ports, and protocols — fast but limited. Stateful inspection firewalls track the state of active connections and make decisions based on context, not just individual packets. Application-layer (proxy) firewalls inspect traffic at the application level, understanding protocols like HTTP and FTP, providing deeper security. Next-generation firewalls combine all these with features like intrusion prevention, deep packet inspection, and application awareness.
questions.followUp: How does a stateful firewall differ from a stateless packet filter?

questions.question: Explain the HTTP request-response cycle and common HTTP methods.
questions.idealAnswer: HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol. A client sends a request with a method, URL, headers, and optional body. The server processes it and returns a response with a status code, headers, and body. Common methods: GET retrieves data (idempotent, no body), POST creates resources (has body), PUT updates/replaces resources (idempotent, has body), DELETE removes resources (idempotent), PATCH partially updates resources. Status codes: 200 (OK), 201 (Created), 301 (Redirect), 400 (Bad Request), 401 (Unauthorized), 404 (Not Found), 500 (Server Error). Each request is independent — the server retains no state between requests unless using cookies or sessions.

oop.description: Classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstraction, design patterns, and SOLID principles.

questions.question: Explain the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming.
questions.idealAnswer: The four pillars of OOP are: Encapsulation — bundling data and methods that operate on that data within a single unit (class), restricting direct access to internal state through access modifiers (private, protected, public). Abstraction — hiding complex implementation details and exposing only essential features through abstract classes and interfaces. Inheritance — creating new classes that derive from existing ones, inheriting properties and methods for code reuse and establishing is-a relationships. Polymorphism — the ability to treat objects of different classes through a common interface; includes method overriding (runtime polymorphism) and method overloading (compile-time polymorphism).
questions.followUp: Can you give a real-world example demonstrating all four pillars?

questions.question: What are SOLID principles and why are they important?
questions.idealAnswer: SOLID is an acronym for five design principles that promote maintainable and scalable software. Single Responsibility Principle — a class should have only one reason to change. Open/Closed Principle — classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Liskov Substitution Principle — objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of subclasses without breaking functionality. Interface Segregation Principle — clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use. Dependency Inversion Principle — high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. These principles reduce coupling, increase cohesion, and make code easier to test and modify.
questions.followUp: Give an example of how violating the Single Responsibility Principle can cause problems.

questions.question: What is the difference between abstract classes and interfaces?
questions.idealAnswer: An abstract class can have both abstract (unimplemented) and concrete (implemented) methods, instance variables, constructors, and can maintain state. It is extended using inheritance. An interface defines a contract of methods that implementing classes must fulfill. In most languages, a class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one abstract class. Abstract classes are ideal when classes share common implementation and state. Interfaces are ideal for defining capabilities or behaviors that unrelated classes can implement. Modern interfaces (Java 8+, C#) can have default method implementations, blurring the distinction, but interfaces still cannot have instance state.
questions.followUp: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?

questions.question: Explain common design patterns: Singleton, Factory, and Observer.
questions.idealAnswer: Singleton ensures a class has only one instance and provides global access to it, useful for managers, configurations, and connection pools. It uses a private constructor and a static method to return the single instance. Factory Method defines an interface for creating objects but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate, decoupling object creation from usage. It is useful when the exact type of object depends on runtime conditions. Observer defines a one-to-many dependency where when one object (subject) changes state, all its dependents (observers) are notified automatically. It is widely used in event handling systems, UI frameworks, and reactive programming.
questions.followUp: What are the drawbacks of the Singleton pattern?

questions.question: What is method overriding vs method overloading?
questions.idealAnswer: Method overloading (compile-time polymorphism) occurs when multiple methods in the same class share the same name but have different parameter lists (number, type, or order of parameters). The compiler determines which method to call based on the arguments. Method overriding (runtime polymorphism) occurs when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method already defined in its superclass with the same signature. The JVM determines which method to call at runtime based on the actual object type. Overloading enables a method to handle different types of inputs, while overriding enables subclasses to provide specialized behavior.
questions.followUp: Can you override a static method?

questions.question: What is composition vs inheritance? When should you prefer composition?
questions.idealAnswer: Inheritance creates an is-a relationship where a subclass inherits from a superclass. Composition creates a has-a relationship where a class contains instances of other classes and delegates functionality to them. Composition should be preferred when there is no clear is-a relationship, when you need more flexibility (you can change behavior at runtime by swapping composed objects), and to avoid issues like the fragile base class problem and diamond problem in multiple inheritance. The principle 'favor composition over inheritance' promotes loose coupling and greater flexibility. Inheritance is appropriate when there is a genuine is-a hierarchy and you need to reuse a common interface.
questions.followUp: Can you give an example of the fragile base class problem?

questions.question: Explain the concept of coupling and cohesion in software design.
questions.idealAnswer: Coupling measures the degree of interdependence between modules. Low coupling means modules are relatively independent — changes in one don't heavily impact others. High coupling means modules are tightly interconnected, making changes risky and testing difficult. Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities within a single module are. High cohesion means a module focuses on a single, well-defined task. Low cohesion means a module handles many unrelated responsibilities. Good design aims for low coupling and high cohesion — each module does one thing well and has minimal dependencies on other modules, resulting in code that is easier to maintain, test, and reuse.

questions.question: What are generics and why are they useful?
questions.idealAnswer: Generics allow you to write classes, methods, and interfaces that work with any data type while maintaining type safety at compile time. Instead of using Object/any type and casting, you parameterize with a type variable (like T). For example, a generic List<T> can be used as List<String> or List<Integer> without separate implementations. Benefits include type safety (catches type errors at compile time instead of runtime), code reuse (one implementation works for all types), and elimination of casts. Bounded types (like T extends Comparable) restrict the types that can be used. Generics are fundamental to collection frameworks and algorithm libraries.

questions.question: Explain the difference between cookies, local storage, and session storage.
questions.idealAnswer: Cookies are small data pieces (4KB limit) sent with every HTTP request to the server, have expiration dates, and support domain/path scoping. They are ideal for authentication tokens and tracking. Local storage provides larger storage (5-10MB) that persists indefinitely until explicitly cleared, is client-side only (never sent to server), and is accessible across all tabs of the same origin. Session storage is similar to local storage but survives only for the duration of the browser tab session — closing the tab clears the data. Each is suitable for different use cases: cookies for server communication, local storage for persistent client preferences, session storage for temporary tab-specific data.

questions.question: What is the virtual DOM and how does it improve performance in frameworks like React?
questions.idealAnswer: The virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the actual DOM. When state changes in a component, a new virtual DOM tree is created. The framework diffs (compares) the new virtual DOM with the previous one to identify exactly what changed (reconciliation). Only the changed elements are updated in the real DOM, rather than re-rendering the entire page. This is faster because manipulating the real DOM is expensive — it triggers layout, paint, and compositor operations. The virtual DOM also enables batching multiple state changes into a single DOM update. This abstraction allows developers to write code as if the entire page re-renders while the framework efficiently manages minimal actual DOM modifications.
questions.followUp: What are some alternatives to the virtual DOM approach?

questions.question: Explain Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) and why it exists.
questions.idealAnswer: CORS is a security mechanism that allows servers to specify which origins can access their resources. The same-origin policy in browsers prevents scripts from making requests to different origins (different domain, protocol, or port) by default, protecting against attacks like CSRF. CORS relaxes this using HTTP headers — the server includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin to specify allowed origins. For non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, custom headers), the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request to check if the actual request is allowed. The server responds with allowed methods, headers, and credentials policy. CORS enables secure cross-origin communication for APIs while maintaining browser security.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between a simple request and a preflight request?

questions.question: What are closures in JavaScript and how are they used?
questions.idealAnswer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its outer (enclosing) scope even after the outer function has finished executing. This happens because JavaScript functions carry a reference to their lexical environment. Closures are fundamental to JavaScript and used extensively for: data privacy (emulating private variables by exposing only selected functions), callbacks and event handlers (retaining context), function factories (creating specialized functions), and module patterns. For example, a counter function that returns increment/decrement functions, where the count variable is accessible only through those closures, not directly from outside.

questions.question: Explain RESTful API design principles.
questions.idealAnswer: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing web APIs. Key principles include: resource-based URLs (nouns not verbs, like /users/123), standard HTTP methods for operations (GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove), statelessness (each request contains all necessary information), proper HTTP status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found), consistent response formatting (typically JSON), support for filtering, sorting, and pagination through query parameters, and versioning for backwards compatibility. RESTful APIs are predictable, scalable, and easy to consume because they follow standardized conventions.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between REST and GraphQL?

questions.question: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) and how can it be prevented?
questions.idealAnswer: XSS is a security vulnerability where attackers inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. Stored XSS saves malicious scripts in the database (e.g., comments). Reflected XSS reflects malicious input from the URL back into the page. DOM-based XSS manipulates the client-side DOM. Prevention includes: input validation and sanitization on both client and server, output encoding/escaping (converting special characters to HTML entities), Content Security Policy (CSP) headers to restrict script sources, using framework features that auto-escape output (React JSX), HttpOnly cookies to prevent script access to session cookies, and avoiding innerHTML with user data.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between XSS and CSRF attacks?

questions.question: Explain the event loop in JavaScript and how asynchronous operations work.
questions.idealAnswer: JavaScript is single-threaded but handles async operations through the event loop. The call stack executes synchronous code. When an async operation (setTimeout, fetch, DOM events) is encountered, it is offloaded to Web APIs. When the async operation completes, its callback is placed in the callback queue. The event loop continuously checks if the call stack is empty, and if so, moves callbacks from the queue to the stack. There are two queues: the microtask queue (Promises, queueMicrotask) which has higher priority, and the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O). After each task, all microtasks are processed before the next macrotask, which is why Promises resolve before setTimeout callbacks.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?

questions.question: What is responsive web design and how do you implement it?
questions.idealAnswer: Responsive web design makes websites adapt to different screen sizes and devices. Implementation techniques include: viewport meta tag to control scaling on mobile devices, media queries to apply different styles at specific breakpoints, fluid layouts using percentage-based widths and relative units (rem, em, vw, vh), CSS Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts and CSS Grid for two-dimensional layouts, responsive images using max-width: 100% or the picture element with srcset, and mobile-first approach where you design for small screens first and enhance for larger ones. The goal is a seamless experience across desktops, tablets, and phones without separate codebases.

questions.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
questions.idealAnswer: Supervised learning uses labeled training data (input-output pairs) where the model learns to map inputs to known outputs. It includes classification (predicting discrete categories like spam/not spam) and regression (predicting continuous values like house prices). Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data where the model discovers hidden patterns and structures without predefined outputs. It includes clustering (grouping similar data points like customer segmentation), dimensionality reduction (PCA), and association rule learning. Supervised learning requires human effort to label data but produces precise predictions. Unsupervised learning works with raw data but provides exploratory insights rather than specific predictions.
questions.followUp: What is semi-supervised learning?

questions.question: Explain the bias-variance tradeoff in machine learning.
questions.idealAnswer: The bias-variance tradeoff describes the balance between two sources of error in machine learning models. Bias is error from overly simple assumptions — high bias causes underfitting, where the model fails to capture underlying patterns (too simple). Variance is error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in training data — high variance causes overfitting, where the model learns noise instead of signal (too complex). The tradeoff means reducing bias typically increases variance and vice versa. The goal is finding the sweet spot that minimizes total error. Techniques like cross-validation help evaluate this balance, while regularization (L1, L2) penalizes complexity to reduce variance without excessively increasing bias.
questions.followUp: How do ensemble methods like Random Forest address the bias-variance tradeoff?

questions.question: What is gradient descent and how does it work in training neural networks?
questions.idealAnswer: Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm that minimizes the loss function by updating model parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient (steepest descent). At each step, it computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight using backpropagation, then updates weights by subtracting the gradient multiplied by the learning rate. Variants include batch gradient descent (uses entire dataset), stochastic gradient descent (uses one sample at a time), and mini-batch gradient descent (uses small batches). The learning rate controls step size — too large causes overshooting, too small causes slow convergence. Advanced optimizers like Adam adaptively adjust learning rates per parameter.

questions.question: Explain the architecture of a convolutional neural network (CNN).
questions.idealAnswer: CNNs are deep learning models designed for processing structured grid data like images. The architecture typically consists of: Convolutional layers that apply learned filters (kernels) to input to create feature maps, detecting patterns like edges, textures, and shapes. ReLU activation introduces non-linearity. Pooling layers (max or average pooling) reduce spatial dimensions while retaining important features, providing translation invariance. Multiple convolutional and pooling layers are stacked, with early layers detecting simple features and deeper layers detecting complex patterns. Fully connected layers at the end combine features for final classification. Key parameters include filter size, stride, and padding. CNNs excel at image recognition, object detection, and computer vision tasks.
questions.followUp: What is transfer learning and how is it used with CNNs?

questions.question: What is overfitting and what techniques can be used to prevent it?
questions.idealAnswer: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too well, including noise and outliers, resulting in high training accuracy but poor performance on unseen data. Prevention techniques include: regularization (L1/L2 penalties on weights to discourage complexity), dropout (randomly deactivating neurons during training), cross-validation (evaluating model on different data splits), early stopping (stopping training when validation performance stops improving), data augmentation (increasing training data variety), reducing model complexity (fewer layers/parameters), ensemble methods (combining multiple models), and collecting more diverse training data. The key indicator is a large gap between training and validation performance.
questions.followUp: How does L1 regularization differ from L2 regularization?

questions.question: Explain precision, recall, F1-score, and when each metric is most important.
questions.idealAnswer: Precision is the ratio of true positives to all predicted positives (TP / (TP + FP)) — it measures how accurate positive predictions are. Recall is the ratio of true positives to all actual positives (TP / (TP + FN)) — it measures how many actual positives were correctly identified. F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics. Precision is most important when false positives are costly (spam filtering — don't want to block legitimate emails). Recall is most important when false negatives are costly (disease detection — don't want to miss actual cases). F1-score is useful when you need a balance and the dataset is imbalanced (where accuracy alone is misleading).
questions.followUp: What is the ROC curve and AUC score?

questions.question: What is natural language processing (NLP) and what are its key techniques?
questions.idealAnswer: NLP enables computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Key techniques include: tokenization (splitting text into words/subwords), text preprocessing (stemming, lemmatization, stop word removal), feature extraction (TF-IDF, bag of words, word embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe that capture semantic meaning), sentiment analysis (determining opinion polarity), named entity recognition (identifying names, dates, locations), text classification, machine translation, and question answering. Modern NLP predominantly uses transformer architecture with self-attention mechanisms. Pre-trained language models like BERT (bidirectional encoding) and GPT (generative) have revolutionized NLP by learning rich language representations from massive text corpora and enabling transfer learning.

questions.question: Explain the concept of feature engineering and its importance in machine learning.
questions.idealAnswer: Feature engineering is the process of using domain knowledge to create, transform, and select the most relevant features from raw data to improve model performance. Techniques include: feature creation (combining existing features, extracting date components), feature transformation (log transform for skewed data, polynomial features), feature scaling (normalization to 0-1 range, standardization to zero mean), categorical encoding (one-hot encoding, label encoding), handling missing values (imputation), feature selection (removing irrelevant or redundant features using correlation, mutual information, or recursive elimination), and dimensionality reduction (PCA). Good feature engineering often matters more than model choice and can dramatically improve performance.

questions.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling? When would you use each?
questions.idealAnswer: Vertical scaling (scale up) means adding more power (CPU, RAM) to an existing machine. It is simple but has a hard limit and usually requires downtime. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more machines to your pool of resources. It provides better fault tolerance and infinite scaling but introduces complexity like distributed state and load balancing.

questions.question: Explain what a Load Balancer is and what algorithms it can use.
questions.idealAnswer: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. This ensures no single server bears too much demand, improving responsiveness and availability. Common algorithms include Round Robin (requests distributed sequentially), Least Connections (sent to the server with fewest active connections), and IP Hash (determines server based on client IP).

questions.question: What is caching and what are common caching strategies?
questions.idealAnswer: Caching stores copies of frequently accessed data in a fast storage layer (like RAM) to serve future requests faster. Strategies include Cache Aside (application checks cache, if miss, loads from DB and updates cache), Write Through (data is written to cache and DB simultaneously), and Write Behind (written to cache first, asynchronously to DB). Eviction policies like LRU (Least Recently Used) manage cache size limits.

questions.question: Explain the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer.
questions.idealAnswer: String is immutable, meaning any modification creates a new object, which is inefficient for heavy string manipulation. StringBuilder and StringBuffer are mutable. The difference is that StringBuffer is synchronized (thread-safe) but slower, while StringBuilder is not synchronized and therefore faster for single-threaded operations.
questions.followUp: Why are Strings designed to be immutable in Java?

questions.question: How does Garbage Collection work in Java?
questions.idealAnswer: Java Garbage Collection automatically manages memory by reclaiming space used by unreachable objects. It typically uses a generational approach (Young, Old/Tenured generations). Most objects are created in the Young generation (Eden space). When it fills, a minor GC runs, moving surviving objects to Survivor spaces, and eventually to the Old generation. The Mark and Sweep algorithm is commonly used to identify and remove unreferenced objects.
